19713.sourceSearchName: angular template driven form angular template driven form
19713.title: Angular Template-Driven Form
19713.heading: Angular Template-Driven Form
19713.content:
An Angular template-driven form defines much of its structure and validation through directives in the HTML template. Angular derives the form model from that markup and synchronizes it with component data.

The approach is concise for small forms, but complex rules and dynamic behavior can become distributed through the template. An [[Angular Reactive Form]] instead builds the form model explicitly in TypeScript.

19715.title: Angular Similarity Coordinate
19715.heading: Document

19716.sourceSearchName: angular similarity coordinate angular similarity coordinate
19716.title: Angular Similarity Coordinate
19716.heading: Angular Similarity Coordinate
19716.content:
An angular similarity coordinate represents how alike network nodes are in a hyperbolic embedding. Nodes with nearby angles share latent characteristics, while their radial coordinates separately express popularity or hierarchy.

Combining angle with the [[Radial Popularity Coordinate]] lets [[Hyperbolic Distance]] balance similarity and prominence. Link likelihood generally increases as the resulting distance decreases.

19717.title: Angular Similarity Coordinate

19719.title: Angular Routing
19719.heading: Angular Routing
19719.content:
Angular routing maps browser-side URL patterns to client components. It lets a [[Single-Page Application]] preserve meaningful navigation and location while changing views without requesting a complete replacement page from the server.

In a combined application, server middleware first handles static files and mapped API endpoints; an SPA fallback can then pass remaining paths to Angular so its routing rules select the client view.

19721.sourceSearchName: angular service worker angular service worker
19721.title: Angular Service Worker
19721.heading: Document

19722.sourceSearchName: angular service worker angular service worker
19722.title: Angular Service Worker
19722.heading: Angular Service Worker
19722.content:
The Angular service worker is the framework-supported service-worker implementation supplied through the `@angular/service-worker` package. It integrates generated application bundles with configurable caching and update behavior.

An Angular application imports the service-worker module for production use and supplies a [[Service Worker Configuration]]. The framework can add the required package and files automatically or they can be configured manually.

19723.sourceSearchName: angular service worker angular service worker
19723.title: Angular Service Worker
19723.heading: References

19725.title: Angular Service
19725.heading: Angular Service
19725.content:
An Angular service is an injectable class that provides reusable behavior outside a component's presentation logic. Services commonly centralize HTTP access, error handling, retry behavior, or shared state.

A component receives the service through [[Dependency Injection]] rather than constructing it. This makes the component smaller and allows a [[Mock Object|mock service]] to replace network behavior during a unit test.

19727.sourceSearchName: angular reactive form angular reactive form
19727.title: Angular Reactive Form
19727.heading: Document

19728.sourceSearchName: angular reactive form angular reactive form
19728.title: Angular Reactive Form
19728.heading: Angular Reactive Form
19728.content:
An Angular reactive form defines controls, groups, values, and validation rules as an explicit model in component code. The template binds to that model instead of creating the model implicitly from markup.

This model-driven approach gives the developer direct control and a clearer separation between the application's data model and the [[Form Model]]. It also exposes observable value and status changes for validation and debugging.

19729.title: Angular Reactive Form

19731.title: Angular Momentum
19731.heading: Angular Momentum
19731.content: Angular momentum describes rotational motion. For a point particle about an origin, $L=r\times p$; for a rigid body rotating about a fixed principal axis, $L=I\omega$. The resultant external [[Torque]] equals $dL/dt$, making angular momentum the rotational counterpart of linear momentum.

19734.title: Angular Module
19734.heading: Angular Module
19734.content:
An Angular module groups related components, directives, pipes, and imported capabilities into a coherent unit. Module metadata declares what belongs to the unit and what external features it depends on.

The root module bootstraps the application, while feature or utility modules can collect narrower responsibilities such as routing, reactive forms, HTTP communication, or Angular Material controls.

19737.title: Angular Material
19737.heading: Angular Material
19737.content:
Angular Material is a collection of Angular user-interface modules and components. Applications import only the modules they need, such as table, paginator, sort, or select controls, and combine them with application-specific data and behavior.

The library supplies presentation and interaction primitives rather than the data source itself. An [[Angular Material Table]] still depends on a component or service to fetch, page, sort, and filter API results.

19740.title: Angular Material Table
19740.heading: Angular Material Table
19740.content:
An Angular Material table renders structured rows and columns from a component-provided data source. Column definitions connect named fields to headers and cells, while paginator and sort modules add controls around the displayed data.

For large datasets, the table should display the page returned by [[Server-Side Paging]] instead of binding every database row. A loading state can hide or replace the table while the request is unresolved.

19743.title: Angular HttpClient
19743.heading: Angular HttpClient
19743.content:
Angular HttpClient is the framework service used to issue HTTP requests and receive typed responses. It is injected into a component or [[Angular Service]] and can request JSON from an ASP.NET Core [[Web API]].

HttpClient returns an [[Observable]] rather than the final value itself. The consumer subscribes to the asynchronous result and handles returned data or errors when the response arrives.

19745.heading: Document

19746.sourceSearchName: angular form group angular form group
19746.title: Angular Form Group
19746.heading: Angular Form Group
19746.content:
An Angular form group collects named form controls into one reactive structure. Its value is assembled from child values, and its status reflects the validation state of the group and its members.

Grouping lets a component submit or inspect a form as one model while retaining field-level errors. An [[Angular Form Builder]] provides a shorter syntax for constructing groups and controls.

19747.title: Angular Form Group
19747.heading: References

19748.title: Angular Form Control
19748.heading: Document

19749.sourceSearchName: angular form control angular form control
19749.title: Angular Form Control
19749.heading: Angular Form Control
19749.content:
An Angular form control represents one field within a reactive [[Form Model]]. It holds the field's current value and validation status and can publish changes over time.

Validators are attached to the control so the model can distinguish valid and invalid input before submission. Related controls are collected within an [[Angular Form Group]].

19752.title: Angular Form Builder
19752.heading: Angular Form Builder
19752.content:
Angular FormBuilder is an injectable helper for creating reactive form groups, controls, initial values, and validators with less repetitive construction code. It produces the same kind of explicit [[Form Model]] as direct `FormGroup` and `FormControl` construction.

The builder improves declaration convenience but does not change the separation between model-driven form logic and the HTML template.

19755.sourceSearchName: angular data binding angular data binding
19755.title: Angular Data Binding
19755.heading: Angular Data Binding
19755.content:
Angular data binding connects component state and template output. Interpolation places a value into text, property binding supplies a value to an element or component property, and form binding can also carry user changes back into the model.

Binding allows an [[Angular Component Template]] to describe how data is presented without manually rewriting the document for every change. Directives can repeat rows or conditionally display loading and validation states.

19758.title: Angular Component
19758.heading: Angular Component
19758.content:
An Angular component is a client-side unit that coordinates interface behavior with a view. Its TypeScript class stores state and actions, its [[Angular Component Template|template]] describes rendered markup, and its styles control presentation.

Components can receive injected services, participate in the [[Angular Component Lifecycle]], issue requests through an [[Angular HttpClient]], and expose data for binding in their templates.

19760.title: Angular Component Template
19760.heading: Document

19761.sourceSearchName: angular component template angular component template
19761.title: Angular Component Template
19761.heading: Angular Component Template
19761.content:
An Angular component template is the HTML-based view associated with an [[Angular Component]]. It combines markup with bindings, interpolation, and directives so that component state can determine what the browser displays.

The template should remain focused on presentation. Data fetching, state transitions, and reusable business-facing operations belong in the component class or an injected [[Angular Service]].

19764.sourceSearchName: angular component lifecycle angular component lifecycle
19764.title: Angular Component Lifecycle
19764.heading: Angular Component Lifecycle
19764.content:
The Angular component lifecycle is the sequence of creation, initialization, change handling, and destruction events through which a component passes. Lifecycle hooks let application code respond at defined stages rather than relying on arbitrary timing.

`ngOnInit` is commonly used for initialization after Angular has constructed the component and supplied its dependencies. A component can use that hook to begin an [[Angular HttpClient]] request or subscribe to an [[Observable]].

19767.title: Angle Trisection
19767.heading: Angle Trisection
19767.content:
General angle trisection asks for a straightedge-and-compass construction dividing any angle into three equal parts. Certain angles can be trisected, but no construction works for all angles.

Trisecting a 60-degree angle would require solving an irreducible cubic whose relevant coordinate is not constructible.

19770.heading: Angle of Attack and Critical Stall
19770.content: Angle of attack is the angle between an airfoil's chord line and the relative airflow. Increasing it usually increases lift coefficient until the critical angle is reached, after which widespread separation causes lift to decrease and drag to rise. Stall recovery therefore requires reducing angle of attack, regardless of the aircraft's attitude relative to the horizon.

19773.heading: Angle of Incidence and Wing Twist
19773.content: Angle of incidence is the fixed angle between a wing reference line and the aircraft's longitudinal reference. Wing twist changes that incidence along the span: washout reduces it toward the tip, while wash-in increases it. Washout can help the root stall first and preserve aileron effectiveness as the aircraft nears [[Angle of Attack and Critical Stall]].

19776.heading: Angle Measure in Radians
19776.content: The radian measure of a central angle is the length of its intercepted arc on the [[Unit Circle]]. More generally, an arc of length $s$ on a circle of radius $r$ subtends $\theta=s/r$ radians. A full revolution is $2\pi$ radians, so radians make trigonometric and calculus formulas independent of an arbitrary degree scale.

19779.heading: Angle Between Planes
19779.content:
The angle between two planes is determined by the angle between their normal vectors. If $n_1$ and $n_2$ are normals, then

$$\cos\theta=\frac{n_1\cdot n_2}{\|n_1\|\|n_2\|}.$$

Choosing the acute angle gives the usual dihedral angle; oriented settings may retain a signed or supplementary choice.

19782.title: Angle Addition Identities
19782.heading: Angle Addition Identities
19782.content:
The angle-addition identities express a combined rotation through separate angles:

$$\sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta,$$

$$\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta.$$

Changing the sign of $\beta$ gives the subtraction identities. These formulas generate [[Double-Angle Identities]] and many exact trigonometric values.

19785.title: Anemic Domain Model
19785.heading: Anemic Domain Model
19785.content: An anemic domain model contains data structures and relationships but leaves most behavior elsewhere, often in services, SQL, or database procedures. It can closely mirror a persistence schema while revealing little about what the system actually does. A data model is appropriate when persistence is the only need, but calling it a [[Domain Model]] obscures the absence of domain behavior. Behavior-rich entities instead keep state transitions and [[Entity Invariant]]s near the state they protect.

19788.title: Ancillary Evidence
19788.heading: Ancillary Evidence
19788.content:
Ancillary evidence is information that is not itself the state being estimated but changes how a measurement should be interpreted. Visibility, operating conditions, or sensor context can alter the distribution of a reading given the state.

The sensor model therefore conditions on both the state and the ancillary variable. Incorporating that clue prevents a reading gathered under poor conditions from being treated as though its reliability were unchanged.

19791.title: Analytics Record
19791.heading: Analytics Record
19791.content:
An analytics record is the chosen set of attributes used to represent one instance for analysis. It may mix directly captured fields with derived fields calculated from them. Designing the record defines what distinctions a later algorithm can see.

For a service customer, relevant fields might describe a contract, usage, changes in usage, life-cycle stage, or network relationships. Domain knowledge guides this selection; highly correlated fields may be redundant. Removing an irrelevant or redundant field can simplify a model and reduce opportunities to fit spurious patterns.

19794.content:
Moving records from a database to a separate analytics server and loading scored results back can dominate a modeling workflow's time. The book describes an experiment in which extracting and preparing data consumed most of model-building time, while extraction and saving consumed most of scoring time for the tested datasets.

This bottleneck explains interest in in-database analysis and distributed processing near stored data. Reducing movement also reduces uncontrolled copies, but it must be balanced against the capabilities and constraints of the chosen storage environment.

19797.heading: Analytical Game Balance
19797.content:
Analytical game balance uses recorded behavior from existing play to find patterns in paths, choices, progression, success, and abandonment. It is backward-looking: the data describes how people have already interacted with the game.

The method requires a playable game and a sufficiently representative sample. Analytics should inform design rather than dictate it, because measurements need context and cannot reveal experiences or possibilities they were not built to capture.

19800.title: Analytics Base Table
19800.heading: Analytics Base Table
19800.content:
An analytics base table is the assembled dataset supplied to a machine-learning algorithm. Each row is one analytics record, and the columns implement the attributes selected for the task. Its construction usually requires extracting, cleaning, standardizing, transforming, and integrating data from several sources.

The table is not merely a copy of an operational database. It embodies decisions about the unit of analysis, usable time period, target definition, feature construction, and duplicate handling. These choices can affect a model more than the eventual algorithm choice.

19803.title: Analytic Metadata
19803.heading: Analytic Metadata
19803.content:
Analytic metadata records the information needed to interpret and reuse a prepared dataset: variable names, classes, roles, labels, units, transformations, exclusions, and target definitions. It turns implicit script knowledge into an explicit contract.

Saving metadata with the data and partition information supports consistent modeling and later scoring.

19806.sourceSearchName: analytic file export analytic file export
19806.title: Analytic File Export
19806.heading: Analytic File Export
19806.content:
Analytic file export writes the validated in-memory dataset to a stable, portable file used by later analysis scripts. CSV is a common choice because it can be read by many statistical and spreadsheet tools without proprietary software.

Using a consistent output name lets the descriptive and regression stages always load the current analytic data. Intermediate versions may also be exported when several programmers need checkpoints, but the authoritative final file should be produced by code rather than manual editing.

19807.sourceSearchName: analytic file export analytic file export
19807.title: Analytic File Export
19807.heading: References

19809.title: Analytic Dataset
19809.heading: Analytic Dataset
19809.content:
An analytic dataset contains the observations and variables required to answer a specified research question. It operationalizes the target population, exposure, outcome, candidate confounders, missing-data rules, and any constructed measures used by the planned analysis.

The dataset should be produced by a reproducible sequence of selection and recoding steps, then validated and written under a stable name. A later analysis can begin by reading that named file, ensuring that tables and models use the current version rather than an accidental intermediate object.

In the data science setting, the same design is often called an analytics base table: each row is an analytics record and each column is a selected raw or derived attribute. The choice of records, time period, target, and redundant features shapes what a learning algorithm can discover. This extends the health-analysis use case without changing its original definition.

An analogous palette uses neighboring hues on the color wheel. Their shared components create harmony, making the scheme useful for environments that need a continuous mood or gradual transition.

One hue can dominate while the others support variation, preventing the scene from becoming visually flat. Value and saturation differences remain important for separating objects and routes even when the hues themselves are closely related.

19821.title: Analog Fire-Control Computing
19821.heading: Analog Fire-Control Computing
19821.content:
Analog fire-control systems represented equations of motion directly through electrical or mechanical relationships. Continuously changing radar and tracking inputs adjusted a computed firing solution in real time.

These systems succeeded before general digital computers were practical. Their design raised lasting questions about feedback, automatic control, and how human operators should interact with fast machinery.

19824.title: Analog Input Filtering
19824.heading: Analog Input Filtering
19824.content:
Analog input filtering removes small, unintended, or noisy values from an [[Analog Input Device]]. A dead zone can map values near the neutral position to zero, while rescaling preserves useful control across the remaining range.

Filtering prevents drift and unstable motion. The chosen threshold must be large enough to suppress hardware noise without erasing deliberate subtle input.

19825.heading: References

19827.title: Analog Input Device
19827.heading: Analog Input Device
19827.content:
An analog input device reports a value over a range rather than a single on-or-off state. Thumbsticks, triggers, and motion sensors can express direction or intensity in addition to activation.

Raw values often contain noise or small unwanted deviations. [[Analog Input Filtering]] converts them into stable control values before gameplay interprets them.

Analog computing represents a quantity through a continuously varying physical quantity, while digital computing represents it with discrete symbols. A mechanical cam shaped like an equation is analog; a numerical procedure executed with pulses is digital.

The categories were not sharply named until the 1930s and often coexisted in early systems. Digital methods prevailed because discrete states were easier to copy, control, and combine reliably at electronic speed.

Ampere's law relates the circulation of magnetic field around a closed path to enclosed current:

For highly symmetric steady-current arrangements, it provides direct fields for a long straight wire or solenoid. The more general Maxwell form also includes changing electric flux.

19839.title: Ambiguous Grammar
19839.heading: Ambiguous Grammar
19839.content:
A context-free grammar is ambiguous when at least one generated string has more than one left derivation, equivalently more than one [[Parse Tree]]. The alternatives can assign genuinely different structures and meanings to the same terminal sequence.

Arithmetic grammars avoid ambiguity by separating expressions, terms, and factors so that precedence and grouping are encoded in the grammar. Removing ambiguity is important for compilers because a parser must choose a definite program structure.

19842.title: Ambiguity Resolution
19842.heading: Ambiguity Resolution
19842.content:
Ambiguity resolution selects among multiple plausible interpretations of a user's input. Evidence can come from recognition confidence, syntax, domain knowledge, prior turns, personal context, and available actions.

When the evidence is insufficient, the safest resolution is often a [[Clarification Question]]. The cost of an extra turn should be weighed against the consequence of executing the wrong service action.

Eevee uses ambient occlusion as a screen-space effect, while Cycles already calculates broader global illumination and usually has less need for the approximation. Factor and distance settings control its strength and reach.

19848.title: Alternative Clustering
19848.heading: Alternative Clustering
19848.content:
Alternative clustering searches for a valid partition that is meaningfully different from a previously known or dominant clustering. The goal is not merely to perturb assignments but to reveal another coherent organization of the same observations.

Difference can be imposed on memberships, feature directions, pairwise relationships, or information shared with the reference partition. A useful alternative must satisfy both novelty and quality; maximizing disagreement alone produces arbitrary groups.

The separation supports parallel and distributed computation because many user or item updates can be calculated independently during each phase. Iteration continues until improvement or another stopping criterion is reached.

19866.title: Alpha-Investing Feature Selection
19866.heading: Alpha-Investing Feature Selection
19866.content:
Alpha-investing feature selection treats sequential feature tests as investments from a changing statistical wealth. Accepting a useful feature can replenish the budget, while testing candidates spends it.

The procedure is suited to streaming dimensions because it makes an immediate inclusion decision while controlling the accumulation of false discoveries. Its behavior depends on the order of arriving features and on how aggressively the available testing wealth is allocated.

In streaming feature engineering, alpha-investing provides a principled stopping and acceptance mechanism when the number of future candidates is unknown. Statistical wealth links each decision to the history of earlier tests.

19875.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning
19875.heading: Alpha-Beta Pruning
19875.content:
Alpha-beta pruning accelerates [[Minimax]] by abandoning branches that cannot change the final decision. Alpha tracks the best value already guaranteed to the maximizing player, and beta tracks the best value guaranteed to the minimizing player.

When a branch proves no better than an established alternative, its remaining descendants need not be evaluated. The result is identical to ordinary minimax, but good move ordering can reduce the number of searched nodes dramatically.

19878.title: Alpha Milestone
19878.heading: Alpha Milestone
19878.content:
The alpha milestone is a checkpoint at which a game is largely playable and its major systems, features, and assets are present. Important bugs may remain, but the core and secondary gameplay have been tested beyond the development team.

After alpha, emphasis shifts from adding major features toward balancing, testing, and fixing. Treating alpha as a [[Stage Gate]] forces the team to judge the game's actual experience rather than continue solely because much work has already been invested.

19887.heading: Alpha Blending in OpenGL
19887.content:
Alpha blending in OpenGL combines a source fragment with the color already stored in the framebuffer according to configured blend factors. A common rule weights the source by its alpha and the destination by one minus source alpha.

Blending makes sprite transparency and translucent surfaces possible, but draw order matters because the operation is generally not commutative. Transparent geometry is usually rendered after opaque geometry and often requires back-to-front sorting.

19902.title: Algorithmic Privacy
19902.heading: Algorithmic Privacy
19902.content:
Algorithmic privacy concerns the effects of automated analysis on a person's control over information and exposure. A system can threaten privacy without publishing a secret: it may combine ordinary traces, infer sensitive characteristics, predict behavior, or make consequential classifications invisible to the person involved.

Protection therefore covers both data and processing. People need intelligible information about automated use, safeguards against inappropriate reuse, and ways to challenge decisions. [[Meaningful Digital Consent]] helps, but it cannot carry the entire burden when collection is pervasive or participation in digital infrastructure is difficult to avoid.

19905.title: Algorithmic Heuristic
19905.heading: Algorithmic Heuristic
19905.content:
An algorithmic heuristic is a strategy for choosing among alternative moves while constructing a solution. It narrows the search by applying a practical rule rather than exploring every possible continuation.

A [[Greedy Algorithm]] uses the heuristic of selecting the best-looking immediate option. The result may be excellent, approximate, or trapped at a [[Local Optimum]], so a heuristic should be evaluated by the guarantees and typical performance it provides for its specific problem.

19907.sourceSearchName: algorithmic primitive manipulation algorithmic primitive manipulation
19907.title: Algorithmic Primitive Manipulation
19907.heading: Document

19908.sourceSearchName: algorithmic primitive manipulation algorithmic primitive manipulation
19908.title: Algorithmic Primitive Manipulation
19908.heading: Algorithmic Primitive Manipulation
19908.content:
Algorithmic primitive manipulation creates a model by applying operations such as subdivision, selection, translation, and extrusion to a simple starting shape. The procedure itself becomes the model description, so changing parameters can generate a family of related forms.

This approach is natural when parameterization is the goal, as with a maze, fence, or architectural element whose dimensions and repetitions vary. It is inefficient when a highly detailed asset is effectively fixed and only needs simple resizing; in that case, loading an interchange file preserves detail with much less code.

19909.sourceSearchName: algorithmic primitive manipulation algorithmic primitive manipulation
19909.title: Algorithmic Primitive Manipulation
19909.heading: References

19911.title: Algorithmic Neutrality
19911.heading: Algorithmic Neutrality
19911.content:
Algorithmic neutrality is the claim that an automated system merely applies objective mathematics and is therefore independent of social values. The claim is misleading because choices about data, categories, targets, error costs, and deployment determine what the system represents and whose interests it serves.

An algorithm can apply a rule consistently while reproducing an unjust institution or unequal history. Recognizing non-neutrality does not mean that every result is arbitrary. It means assumptions should be documented and justified rather than hidden behind technical language. [[Algorithmic Accountability]] begins where the appearance of inevitability ends.

19914.title: Algorithmic Fairness
19914.heading: Algorithmic Fairness
19914.content:
Algorithmic fairness is the demand that automated decisions distribute treatment, errors, opportunities, and burdens in a justifiable way. It may be evaluated through equal treatment, equal outcomes, comparable error rates, protection of rights, or attention to existing disadvantage.

These aims can conflict, especially when groups differ because of historical conditions. Selecting a metric therefore expresses a theory of justice rather than removing values from the decision. Fairness work must state which people and outcomes matter, explain why a criterion is appropriate, and examine whether the institution using the system is itself legitimate.

19917.title: Algorithmic Bias
19917.heading: Algorithmic Bias
19917.content:
Algorithmic bias is a systematic tendency for an automated system to produce distorted or unequally harmful outcomes. Bias can enter through the population sampled, labels, variables, model objective, deployment data, or the way people interpret and act on the output.

The source is not always a prejudiced programmer. A model trained on historical practice may accurately reproduce an unjust pattern, and an apparently neutral variable may act as a social proxy. Because bias can emerge throughout the [[Data Science Pipeline]], mitigation requires technical testing together with judgment about which differences are ethically relevant.

19919.title: Algorithmic Discrimination

Tags: [[Algorithmic Fairness and Justice]] · [[Big Data Law and Individual Rights]]

19920.title: Algorithmic Discrimination
19920.heading: Algorithmic Discrimination
19920.content:
Algorithmic discrimination occurs when an automated decision produces unjust disadvantage for a person or group. The system may distinguish people directly through a protected characteristic or indirectly through variables that reproduce the same social division.

Not every distinction is unjust: some decisions legitimately use relevant differences, and corrective policies may intentionally consider group membership. The ethical question is therefore not whether an algorithm treats everyone identically, but whether its criteria and effects can be justified under an appropriate account of [[Algorithmic Fairness]]. Evidence of unequal outcomes must be interpreted in the social and institutional context where the system operates.

Large-scale profiling can discriminate through inferred group membership even when protected characteristics are not explicit inputs. The relevant legal and social analysis must therefore examine collective effects and the opportunities or burdens produced by the decision system.

19923.sourceSearchName: algorithmic due process algorithmic due process
19923.title: Algorithmic Due Process
19923.heading: Algorithmic Due Process
19923.content:
Algorithmic due process applies procedural fairness to decisions made or supported by automated systems. A person affected by a consequential decision should know that automation was used, understand the relevant basis, receive a comprehensible reason, and have a real opportunity to challenge errors.

The requirement connects [[Right to Explanation]] with institutional remedy. Disclosure without appeal leaves the person's position unchanged, while an appeal without adequate information cannot test the system's reasoning. Due process also requires a responsible human or organization with authority to review and correct the outcome rather than treating the model as final.

19926.title: Algorithmic Auditability
19926.heading: Algorithmic Auditability
19926.content:
Algorithmic auditability is the capacity of an AI system and its surrounding process to be examined by an authorized reviewer. An audit may evaluate training data, model construction, performance across groups, security, records of use, and whether required procedures were followed.

Auditability must be designed in advance because evidence that was never recorded cannot be reconstructed reliably after harm. It differs from public [[AI Transparency]]: some audits require protected access to sensitive data or proprietary systems. The ethical value comes from connecting evidence to standards, consequences, and actors able to require change.

19929.title: Algorithmic and Mathematical Thinking
19929.heading: Algorithmic and Mathematical Thinking
19929.content:
Algorithmic thinking differs from mathematical thinking by emphasizing executable processes, information structures, changing state, and reductions of complex tasks into connected simple operations. It also moves deliberately among levels of abstraction.

Mathematical proof remains important, but a computational designer must additionally invent representations and notations that a machine can act on. The concern is not only whether a relationship is true, but how a process realizes it.

19932.title: Algorithmic Accountability
19932.heading: Algorithmic Accountability
19932.content:
Algorithmic accountability is the requirement that people and organizations using automated systems remain answerable for their design choices, decisions, and consequences. It includes identifying who can authorize use, who monitors performance, who explains an outcome, and who can provide correction or remedy.

Accountability is broader than [[AI Transparency]]. Information must reach an actor with both a duty to respond and the power to change the system. Clear roles, [[Algorithmic Auditability]], complaint procedures, and enforceable rules prevent distributed development from becoming a [[Responsibility Gap]].

19935.title: Algorithm Output
19935.heading: Algorithm Output
19935.content:
An algorithm's output is the result produced after its steps process an [[Algorithm Input]]. The output represents the proposed solution to the problem, such as a greatest common divisor, a sorted permutation, a shortest path, or a classification.

Producing a value is not enough to establish that it is useful. The input must meet the [[Algorithm]]'s requirements, the implementation must preserve its steps, and the result must be interpreted according to the problem the algorithm was designed to solve.

19938.title: Algorithm
19938.heading: Algorithm
19938.content:
An algorithm is a precise set of steps for solving a problem or carrying out a task. It can be followed by a person with pencil and paper or expressed as a [[Program]] for a computer; computers make algorithms fast, but they do not define what an algorithm is.

An algorithm may receive an [[Algorithm Input]], transforms that data through operations arranged by a [[Control Structure]], and produces an [[Algorithm Output]]. Its steps must be unambiguous, effective, and guaranteed to finish after a finite amount of work.

19941.title: Algorithm Termination
19941.heading: Algorithm Termination
19941.content:
Algorithm termination is the requirement that a procedure finish after a finite number of steps. A repeated operation therefore needs a condition that eventually ends its [[Iteration Control Structure|iteration]] rather than allowing it to continue forever.

Termination distinguishes an [[Algorithm]] from a general computational process. A program may intentionally run indefinitely, but a claimed algorithm must reach an [[Algorithm Output]] for every valid input covered by its definition.

19944.title: Algorithm Input
19944.heading: Algorithm Input
19944.content:
An algorithm's input is the data supplied for processing. It describes the particular instance of a problem: Euclid's algorithm, for example, receives two integers whose greatest common divisor is sought.

Not every [[Algorithm]] needs to receive all its data at once. An [[Online Algorithm]] accepts input incrementally and maintains a result as new items arrive. In either case, the permitted input must satisfy the algorithm's assumptions or its output may be meaningless.

19947.title: Algorithm Family Reuse by Design Patterns
19947.heading: Algorithm Family Reuse by Design Patterns
19947.content:
An algorithm family can reuse architecture when its invariant steps are separated from its variable mathematics. Template Method provides the shared sequence, Strategy supplies replaceable collaborators, and factory-like or prototype operations construct polymorphic components.

The Lance-Williams classes demonstrate this arrangement: all agglomerative variants build and merge the same forest, while each subclass changes only the recurrence used to update intercluster distance.

19956.title: Algorithm Effectiveness
19956.heading: Algorithm Effectiveness
19956.content:
Algorithm effectiveness means that every prescribed step is elementary enough to be carried out exactly in a reasonable amount of time. The method must say what action to perform rather than depend on intuition, revelation, or an operation that cannot actually be completed.

Effectiveness at the step level does not guarantee that the whole [[Algorithm]] is practical. A finite procedure may still require an enormous number of effective steps, which is why [[Computational Complexity]] is evaluated separately.

19959.title: Algebraic Word Problem
19959.heading: Algebraic Word Problem
19959.content:
An algebraic word problem describes quantitative relationships in ordinary language and asks for an unknown value. Solving begins by assigning a variable, expressing every related quantity in terms of it, and translating the stated relationship into an [[Equation]] or inequality.

The symbolic manipulation is only the middle of the process. Units and context guide the model, and the numerical solution must be interpreted and checked against the original situation. Consecutive-number, age, cost, rate, mixture, and sharing problems differ in story but use the same cycle of representation, solution, and verification.

19962.title: Algebraic Term
19962.heading: Algebraic Term
19962.content:
An algebraic term is a component of an [[Algebraic Expression]] separated from other terms by outermost addition or subtraction. It can contain a number, variables, exponents, and products, such as (-4a^2b^3).

The sign belongs to the term, so the expression (a-3b) can be read as the sum of (a) and (-3b). A term's numerical factor is its [[Numerical Coefficient]]. Terms can be combined only when their variable factors and corresponding exponents match, making them [[Like Terms]].

19965.title: Algebraic Simplification
19965.heading: Algebraic Simplification
19965.content:
Algebraic simplification transforms an expression into a more useful equivalent form. Common steps include applying exponent laws, distributing factors, suppressing parentheses, arranging terms, and [[Combining Like Terms]].

Simpler does not always mean shorter in every context. Expansion may expose like terms, while [[Polynomial Factorization]] may expose zeros or permit cancellation. Each step must be justified by an arithmetic property and preserve the expression for all permitted variable values. A cancelled denominator factor still leaves the original restriction that the factor cannot equal zero.

19968.title: Algebraic SI Derived Units
19968.heading: Algebraic SI Derived Units
19968.content: A derived SI unit is built by multiplying or dividing base units. The book's Table 2-2 writes force as the newton, $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$, and pressure as the pascal, $\mathrm{Pa}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$. Special names make frequently used combinations shorter without changing their dimensional structure. Radian and steradian are listed with a unit expression of one because matching lengths or areas cancel. See [[Seven SI Base Units]] and [[Dimensional Homogeneity in Equations]].
